Triggers.value: Difficulty breathing or feeling short of breath
Undergoing a medical examination or procedure

Maladaptive Strategies.value: I think about how life would have been different if the event had not occurred
I tell myself I deserve to suffer because of what happened

Threat.value: I wake during the night to check whether I am safe
My body reacts to danger before I have even had time to think
I only feel safe in a very limited number of places

Negative Appraisals.value: My reactions since the event show that I am a lousy coper
I can't trust that I will do the right thing

issues.explanation: 'Arguments' is a weak fit as a primary trigger for PTSD related to a life-threatening illness when the rest of the profile is dominated by somatic danger cues, hypervigilant threat monitoring, and self-appraisals about coping. It is not impossible, but in this profile it appears disconnected from the illness-centered threat pattern and lacks support from memory/appraisal content.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Restrict Eating: control eating strictly to feel in control
issues.explanation: 'Restrict eating to feel in control' is not well integrated with the rest of the formulation. The active edges emphasize threat and negative appraisals leading to maladaptive strategies, but the other selected strategies are cognitive/self-punitive and illness-related themes are otherwise absent from eating control. In this profile it looks like a strategy addressing a different problem domain unless additional body/illness-control content were present.

vignette:
Mere began to unravel after a life-threatening bout of illness that had started with what she first dismissed as a stubborn chest tightness while she was loading equipment before a rehearsal. By the time she reached the hospital, she was struggling to breathe, and the smell of disinfectant in the corridor became welded in her mind to the panic of not knowing whether she would make it through the night. She remembers the cold of the examination room, the humiliation of being prodded and listened to, and the way her own body seemed to turn against her in front of strangers. Even now, as a 46-year-old musician with a busy life in Australia, she can be thrown off by the faintly clinical smell of a medical office or by the simple act of drawing a full breath when she is singing or climbing stairs; a breathless moment can drop her straight back into that hospital fear, and anything resembling a physical examination feels charged with the same threat.

In the months that followed, Mere began waking in the dark to check whether she was safe, lying still and listening to her breathing before she would let herself settle again. She described her body as reacting before her mind had time to catch up: a flutter in her chest, a sharp intake of breath, a pulse of alarm that seemed to arrive without warning. Those night checks and the constant bodily vigilance made her feel as though there were only a very limited number of places where she could relax at all, and even then she trusted them only briefly. As her sleep became more broken and her sense of safety narrowed, she started to see the illness as proof that she was inadequate, that her reactions since then showed she was a lousy coper, and that she could not trust herself to do the right thing if something happened again. That self-criticism did not stay abstract; it pushed her toward punishing herself with the thought that she deserved to suffer because of what happened, and it fed the painful habit of thinking about how life would have been different if the illness had never occurred.

Those appraisals and the ongoing sense of danger became intertwined in the way Mere managed her days. Because she believed she was not handling things properly and could not rely on her own judgement, she began avoiding hospitals, ambulances, and routine physical examinations, putting off appointments and finding reasons not to go near anything medical unless she absolutely had to. At the same time, her fear that danger could arrive through her body kept her scanning for signs of breathlessness and reacting quickly to any sensation that reminded her of the original illness. If she noticed her breathing change while singing, she would withdraw from rehearsal or move to the edge of the room, telling herself she needed to stay in control. When the smell of antiseptic drifted through a clinic entrance or from a nearby pharmacy, she would turn away before she had fully registered it, already bracing for the old panic. These patterns made it easier, for a moment, to feel less exposed, but they also kept her life moving around the illness rather than away from it.

Over time, that narrowing had concrete costs. As a musician, Mere had once spent much of her week moving between rehearsals, venues, and the occasional performance in unfamiliar places, but now she planned everything around how safe a space felt and how easily she could leave if her body began to alarm her. Her husband had noticed how often she asked to sit near exits or to skip medical checkups she used to manage without fuss. Mere was aware that the more she avoided, the more convinced she became that she truly was fragile and unreliable, and the more she watched her body for warning signs. In the second half of the night, she still woke to check whether she was safe. In the day, the smallest breathless sensation could pull her back to that hospital corridor, and the smell of a procedure room could undo hours of careful composure.

By the time she sought help, Mere was exhausted by how tightly her world had shrunk and frightened by how easily her own body could set everything off. She came in not only because the memories of the illness still felt vivid and dangerous, but because she feared she was becoming a person who would never trust herself or move freely again. What she most hoped for was to breathe, sleep, and work without feeling that every clinic, every smell, and every tightening in her chest meant the danger was back.
